\title{Where do learned decoders actually win?\\
An empirical map of the edge-representability boundary for
surface-code decoders}
\author{Shaun Liebenberg}
\date{November 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
% CLAIM SCOPE: controlled stim experiments, rotated memory-Z, d<=7.
% DO NOT claim quantum advantage, device noise, or production readiness.
We measure when a learned (or data-calibrated) decoder beats
minimum-weight perfect matching on the rotated surface code, and when it
cannot. Two findings. (i) Under any noise the matching graph can
represent, including biased noise at $\eta{=}100$ and 4x rate
miscalibration, MWPM's logical error rate is unchanged; weight
recalibration is a no-op and even an oracle prior buys at most ~2\%.
(ii) Under correlated multi-qubit faults the boundary is real but
asymmetric: a small MLP beats MWPM at $d{=}3$ (1.8\% vs 3.0\%,
McNemar $p{<}0.001$ over three seeds) yet fails at $d{\geq}5$ (13--28\%
vs 4.5--5.4\%), while MWPM degrades gracefully and an oracle prior
improves with distance. The learned win survives scaling only in hybrid
form: a network given MWPM's own prediction as a feature beats MWPM at
$d{=}3$ and $d{=}5$ (McNemar $p{<}10^{-30}$), recovering 29--87\% of
the oracle gap. Learning to correct the classical decoder scales;
learning to decode does not.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Decoder performance is bounded by the decoder's internal noise model.
The claim we test: a learned decoder wins exactly when the true noise
lies outside the matching graph's representable class.

\section{Method}
Noise suite over rotated memory-Z at $d\in\{3,5,7\}$, $r{=}3d$:
depolarising, biased ($\eta{=}100$, uniform and alternating X/Z), and
correlated XX bursts (\textsc{correlated\_error} on neighbouring data
qubits before each measurement block). Learned decoders: a flat MLP, a
space-time CNN, and a hybrid that takes MWPM's own prediction as an
input feature. All decoders decode identical stim-sampled shards;
McNemar paired test on disagreements.
\textbf{Honesty machinery:} zero-noise invariants, calibration with a
held-out validation gate, oracle = MWPM on the true generating DEM.

\section{Results}
\subsection{The dead regime: edge-representable noise}
% Table: depolarising/biased rows, naive ~= calibrated ~= oracle.
Under depolarising and both bias patterns, all three matching variants
are statistically identical at every distance (Table~\ref{tab:edge}).
Fitting weights from syndrome marginals recovers nothing, because there
is nothing to recover: MWPM's insensitivity is structural.

\centering\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
$d$ & naive & calibrated & oracle\\\midrule
3 & $0.0454$ & $0.0454$ & $0.0454$\\
5 & $0.0412$ & $0.0417$ & $0.0415$\\
7 & $0.0307$ & $0.0303$ & $0.0302$\\
\bottomrule\end{tabular}
\caption{Hetero X/Z-bias $\eta{=}100$, $p{=}0.005$, LER (se $\approx$

\subsection{The live regime: correlated bursts}
% Table: burst rows d=3 win, d=5/7 loss; mcnemar; obs rates.
Under $p_{\mathrm{burst}}{=}0.15$, $p_{\mathrm{base}}{=}0.001$: at
$d{=}3$ the MLP recovers $\sim$60\% of the naive-to-oracle gap and beats
MWPM with McNemar $p{<}0.001$ on all seeds. At $d{=}5,7$ the same
recipe overfits (train LER $\sim$0 vs test 13--28\%) and loses
decisively; regularisation removes the overfit and the win together.
Naive MWPM degrades from 3.0\% to 5.4\%; the oracle reaches 0.03--0.4\%,
i.e.\ the value of knowing the noise \emph{grows} with distance.

\subsection{The hybrid result}
Feeding MWPM's prediction to the network as one extra feature flips the
scaling failure: the hybrid beats naive MWPM at $d{=}3$ (1.2\% vs 3.2\%)
\emph{and} $d{=}5$ (3.3\% vs 4.5\%), McNemar $p{<}10^{-30}$ in both
cases, recovering 87\% and 29\% of the naive-to-oracle gap. Starting
from the classical answer is what lets a small learned decoder scale;
decoding from scratch does not.

\subsection{Calibration with a conscience}
Marginal-fitted calibration actively harms under strong correlation
(6.9\% vs 3.1\% at $d{=}3$). A held-out validation gate detects this
and falls back to nominal weights. Any upstream calibration utility
needs this gate.

\section{Discussion}
The boundary is noise-representability, and the learned side of it is
architecture-sensitive: flat decoders win only at the smallest code,
while the hybrid pattern (classical answer in, correction out) wins
through $d{=}5$ and tracks the literature's strongest results.
Marginal reweighting, by contrast, buys nothing in either regime once
validated honestly.

\section{Limitations}
Synthetic noise only; small codes; single learned architecture family
fully exercised. The MLP win at $d{=}3$ is real but should not be
over-read.
